newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major survives vote, faces new business row.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major survives vote, faces new business row.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major's government survived a tight vote over health policy on Tuesday night but was forced onto the defensive in a row about links between leading businessmen and the opposition.
Major's Conservative government, which has lost its overall majority in the House of Commons, won by 319 to 312 with support from some Northern Irish members of parliament.

But the government, which is trailing the opposition Labour party in opinion polls with an election due by May, was criticised by some leading businessmen after Major's deputy Michael Heseltine accused them of supporting Labour.

A defeat in the vote would have been a serious political embarrassment for Major and raised the prospect of his failing to hold on to power until May, although it would not have prompted a confidence motion putting his government at risk.
The Conservatives have been thrown on the defensive by a New Year offensive by the opposition.
Labour wrong-footed Major on Monday with a pledge to hold spending in check and freeze income tax rates if it took power.

Tony Blair, who has dragged Labour from the left to the political centre since he took over as leader in 1994, drove home the message on Tuesday with a pledge not to scrap the free-market reforms introduced by the Conservatives.

Blair used the launch of a report by a commission of businessmen and academics on the competitiveness of British industry to make his pledge, part of a series designed to rid Labour of its old anti-business, tax-and-spend image.

Blair told the launch: "Today I offer business a new deal for the future. The deal is this: we leave intact the main changes of the 1980s in industrial relations and enterprise. And now, together, we address a new agenda for the 21st century."
But deputy prime minister Heseltine demanded an invitation to speak after Blair and criticised the report, which largely endorsed Labour's policies, as seriously flawed.

He went further in media interviews later. "This organisation is a front organisation for the Labour party," Heseltine told reporters after the launch, which was sponsored by the left-leaning Institute for Public Policy Research.
His outburst angered members of the report commission.
Professor George Bain, the head of the London School of Business and chairman of the commission, said he was "flabbergasted" by Heseltine's attack.

"We were rather surprised at his comments, given that the commissioners were drawn from across the political spectrum and represent all sectors of British business," Bain and other commission members said in a letter to the Financial Times.
"We have no party political agenda, our aim is simply to promote British prosperity," they wrote in the letter, published in Wednesday's editions of the newspaper.
Labour strategists were delighted by Heseltine's outburst, which they said showed how rattled the ruling party were by their failure to make inroads in the Labour party's poll lead.
